extracted.intended_audience: scholars, researchers, and graduate students in media studies, sociology, and communication studies
extracted.subtask_description: An academic theory article defining and specifying 'mediatization' as a social process by which media become both integrated into other institutions and constitute an independent institution with their own logic; provides conceptual distinctions, processes, and empirical guidance for studying media's influence on society and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mediatization
rubrics_metrics.description: By the mediatization of society, we understand the process whereby society to an increasing degree is submitted to, or becomes dependent on, the media and their logic. This process is characterized by a duality in that the media have become integrated into the operations of other social institutions, while they also have acquired the status of social institutions in their own right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediatization denotes a sustained, structural change (not merely single mediated events). The extent of submission vs dependence varies across institutions and sectors. Use this definition to distinguish mediatization from shorter-term mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media logic (core components)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'media logic' refers to the institutional and technological modus operandi of the media, including the ways in which media distribute material and symbolic resources and operate with the help of formal and informal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how media format, technologies, and institutional routines shape communication (affecting sender, content, receivers, and social relations). Consider distribution of material/symbolic resources and the formal/informal rules that structure media activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting/primacy-of-form criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Media logic often consists of a formatting logic that determines how material is categorized, the choice of mode of presentation, and the selection and portrayal of social experience (the 'primacy of form over content').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence that form/format (e.g., sound-bites, program formats) shapes content and public discourse. Example: political actors personalizing messages to fit media formats to gain coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four mediatization processes (extension, substitution, amalgamation, accommodation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key processes whereby media change human communication and interaction: (1) extend communication abilities in time and space; (2) substitute social activities formerly face-to-face; (3) instigate an amalgamation of activities (face-to-face + mediated); (4) require actors to adapt behavior to media valuations, formats and routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four processes as analytic lenses when assessing how a given activity or institution has been transformed by media. Provide concrete examples (internet banking=substitution; politicians using sound-bites=accommodation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct (strong) mediatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct mediatization refers to situations where formerly non-mediated activity converts to a mediated form — the activity is performed through interaction with a medium (strong form when the medium becomes a necessary interface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify 'before' and 'after' states (e.g., physical chess → computerized online chess; online banking). Strong mediatization shows clear substitution and novel options that change experience and cultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect (weak) mediatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect mediatization occurs when an activity is increasingly influenced with respect to form, content, or organization by mediagenic symbols or mechanisms, without necessarily converting fully to a mediated form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect more subtle shifts (e.g., merchandising in restaurants influenced by media franchises). Indirect forms are analytically important though less visibly transformative; they often operate alongside direct forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of institutional dependence vs autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which other institutions submit to the media's logic (loss of autonomy) versus simply becoming more dependent on media resources and formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure variations across institutions (politics may adapt language and routines; schools may lose control over knowledge access). Avoid blanket normative assumptions; empirical investigation required to determine degree and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and historical specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediatization is always bound in time and to cultural context; it should be empirically validated through historical, cultural, and sociological analysis rather than treated as a universal, decontextualized process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid technological determinism and one-size-fits-all accounts. Comparative and historically sensitive studies are required; Krotz and Schulz emphasize context dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-universality and geo-cultural scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediatization is primarily a development that has accelerated in modern, highly industrialized (chiefly Western) societies; its influence will vary across regions and cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming mediatization, substantiate that pattern in the specific society or sector studied. Consider globalization’s role in spreading mediatization but expect variation in degree and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mediatization and mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation refers to communication via a medium in a specific act; mediatization refers to a longer-term process whereby institutions and modes of interaction are changed as a consequence of growing media influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate single mediated acts (mediation) with structural change (mediatization). Use the longer-term institutional criteria to identify mediatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical validation and theory-building requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory of mediatization must be well-specified, comprehensive, coherent, relate to other sociological theories, describe overall developmental trends, and prove its usefulness through concrete empirical studies of mediatization in selected areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies that both map macro trends and provide concrete institution- or sector-level analyses (e.g., toys, language, religion). Use mixed historical and sociological methods to validate theoretical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of normative bias (non-normative stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediatization is a non-normative concept; one should not a priori assume mediatization is negative (e.g., inevitable decline of public sphere). Whether consequences are positive or negative requires context-specific analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state normative premises when evaluating consequences. Empirical assessment should precede normative conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic distinction of media logic's different aspects (technological, organizational, commercial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media logic encompasses technological, organizational and (in some contexts) commercial aspects; commercial logics (dominant in North American material) shape formatting and institutional outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregate which aspects of media logic are driving change in a given case — e.g., technological affordances vs commercial incentives vs organizational routines — and avoid over-attributing effects to technology alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes across social dimensions (globalization, individualization, homogenization, nationalization, localization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediatization can facilitate diverse and sometimes contradictory social tendencies — globalization, individualization, homogenization, nationalization, localization — and these can operate simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map which tendencies predominate in particular contexts; use examples (Al-Jazeera → supranational public spheres; blogging/on-line gaming → individualization). Expect loose couplings between local/national/global spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on authenticity and 'liveness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediatization changes relationships between live and mediated performance: mediated versions can attain their own forms and live performances may come to emulate mediated ones, making authenticity conditional rather than absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse shifts in what audiences treat as 'authentic' (e.g., music where primary experience is recording and live performance authenticates it). Consider interdependence rather than hierarchy between mediated and non-mediated forms.
